1.pericope_label: These are now the chief of their fathers, and this is the genealogy of them that went up with me from Babylon, in the reign of Artaxerxes the king. Of the sons of Phinehas; Gershom: of the sons of Ithamar; Daniel: of the sons of David; Hattush. Of the sons of Shechaniah, of the sons of Pharosh; Zechariah: and with him were reckoned by genealogy of the males an hundred and fifty. Of the sons of Pahath–moab; Elihoenai the son of Zerahiah, and with him two hundred males. Of the sons of Shechaniah; the son of Jahaziel, and with him three hundred males.

schools.summary: Ellicott states the rule the list follows, head of house then wider family, and marks a dropped name at the fifth verse from the Greek; Delitzsch counts twelve lay houses, ten of the names identical with the Greek book of Esdras, and diagnoses the doubled and truncated formulas as textual damage.
Gill guards the priestly names, insisting the Daniel here is a priest of the line of Ithamar and not the prophet, who was of royal blood and of Judah.

Clarke gives the chapter's whole argument before touching a word of it and keeps the three men named Shechaniah apart by their fathers' houses; Wesley reads past the count of males to the households behind it.
Henry treats the register as a recruiting poster, names the total of fourteen hundred and ninety-six, and blames the many who stayed behind for loving their ease better than their religion.

debates.question: Why did so few of the exiles go up with Ezra?

positions.position: They loved their ease better than their religion and doubted Jerusalem would better their condition
The question is not pressed; the register is read as a document with names dropped out of it

debates.question: Does the register count only the men who are named?

positions.position: Only males are expressed, but doubtless the women were carried along as the little ones were
Two priests and one of David's house seem to have come without their families

outliers.claim: Warns that the two priestly names do not mean only two priests went up, since twelve chief priests were chosen later to carry the treasure.

themes: These are now the chief of their fathers, and this is the genealogy of them that went up with me from Babylon, in the reign of Artaxerxes the king.
Of the sons of Phinehas; Gershom: of the sons of Ithamar; Daniel: of the sons of David; Hattush.
Of the sons of Shechaniah, of the sons of Pharosh; Zechariah: and with him were reckoned by genealogy of the males an hundred and fifty.
Of the sons of Pahath–moab; Elihoenai the son of Zerahiah, and with him two hundred males.
Of the sons of Shechaniah; the son of Jahaziel, and with him three hundred males.

10.pericope_label: And of the sons of Shelomith; the son of Josiphiah, and with him an hundred and threescore males.

schools.summary: Ellicott marks a name missing from the Hebrew and supplies the Greek reading, of the sons of Bani, Shelomith the son of Josiphiah, which makes Bani the house and Shelomith the man.

themes: And of the sons of Shelomith; the son of Josiphiah, and with him an hundred and threescore males.

13.pericope_label: And of the last sons of Adonikam, whose names are these, Eliphelet, Jeiel, and Shemaiah, and with them threescore males. Of the sons also of Bigvai; Uthai, and Zabbud, and with them seventy males. And I gathered them together to the river that runneth to Ahava; and there abode we in tents three days: and I viewed the people, and the priests, and found there none of the sons of Levi. Then sent I for Eliezer, for Ariel, for Shemaiah, and for Elnathan, and for Jarib, and for Elnathan, and for Nathan, and for Zechariah, and for Meshullam, chief men; also for Joiarib, and for Elnathan, men of understanding.

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the last sons as the younger branches of Adonikam and places Ahava as both river and town, identified with a site some eighty miles from Babylon; Delitzsch totals the register in Hebrew and in Greek, notes the corrupted names of Bigvai's two heads, and reports the moment Ezra found no Levites among the company.
Gill links the river with Adiabene in Assyria and divides the deputation into nine men of rank and two known for good sense.

Clarke denies that Ahava was anything but a river and reads none of the sons of Levi strictly, as meaning no Levites who were not also priests; Wesley agrees and infers that the Levites named earlier in the book had not yet joined.

debates.question: Was Ahava a river, a town, or both?

positions.position: A river only, probably the Diava or Adiava of Adiabene
Both river and town, nine days out from Babylon
A place whose name the river carried, connected with Adiabene

debates.question: What were the two men of understanding chosen for?

positions.position: Good sense and an ability to state a case well
Office: they were teachers, and perhaps priests

outliers.claim: Gives two rival totals for the returning houses, fourteen hundred and ninety-six males in the Hebrew against sixteen hundred and ninety in the Greek, neither counting the priests or the sons of David.

themes: And of the last sons of Adonikam, whose names are these, Eliphelet, Jeiel, and Shemaiah, and with them threescore males.
Of the sons also of Bigvai; Uthai, and Zabbud, and with them seventy males.
And I gathered them together to the river that runneth to Ahava; and there abode we in tents three days: and I viewed the people, and the priests, and found there none of the sons of Levi.

Then sent I for Eliezer, for Ariel, for Shemaiah, and for Elnathan, and for Jarib, and for Elnathan, and for Nathan, and for Zechariah, and for Meshullam, chief men; also for Joiarib, and for Elnathan, men of understanding.

17.pericope_label: And I sent them with commandment unto Iddo the chief at the place Casiphia, and I told them what they should say unto Iddo, and to his brethren the Nethinims, at the place Casiphia, that they should bring unto us ministers for the house of our God. And by the good hand of our God upon us they brought us a man of understanding, of the sons of Mahli, the son of Levi, the son of Israel; and Sherebiah, with his sons and his brethren, eighteen; And Hashabiah, and with him Jeshaiah of the sons of Merari, his brethren and their sons, twenty; Also of the Nethinims, whom David and the princes had appointed for the service of the Levites, two hundred and twenty Nethinims: all of them were expressed by name.

schools.summary: Ellicott puts Casiphia near Ahava as a Jewish colony under Iddo, takes ministers to cover Levites and Nethinim together, argues that a man of understanding is the proper name Ishsekel, and denies that the men were expressed by name because they were famous; Delitzsch agrees about the name and describes the Nethinim by their office rather than their descent.

Gill rejects the Caspian reading of Casiphia as too distant for the errand and, following Jarchi, places it in or beside Babylon; he leaves the descent of the Nethinim from the Gibeonites an open question.
Clarke holds for the Caspian mountains and suggests the Nethinim were working silver mines there; Wesley turns the good hand of our God into a rule for every supplied vacancy in the ministry.

positions.position: The Caspian mountains between Media and Hyrcania, where the name suggests silver mines
In or beside Babylon; the Caspian is too far for the messengers to go and return in time
Near Ahava, a Jewish colony presided over by Iddo

debates.question: What does all of them were expressed by name mean?

positions.position: They were men of note, distinguished by name
Not that they were famous, but that Iddo sent a list of names the narrative does not reproduce

outliers.claim: Points out that this verse is the only place in scripture recording that David appointed the Nethinim to aid the Levites.

themes: And I sent them with commandment unto Iddo the chief at the place Casiphia, and I told them what they should say unto Iddo, and to his brethren the Nethinims, at the place Casiphia, that they should bring unto us ministers for the house of our God.
And by the good hand of our God upon us they brought us a man of understanding, of the sons of Mahli, the son of Levi, the son of Israel; and Sherebiah, with his sons and his brethren, eighteen;
And Hashabiah, and with him Jeshaiah of the sons of Merari, his brethren and their sons, twenty;
Also of the Nethinims, whom David and the princes had appointed for the service of the Levites, two hundred and twenty Nethinims: all of them were expressed by name.

21.pericope_label: Then I proclaimed a fast there, at the river of Ahava, that we might afflict ourselves before our God, to seek of him a right way for us, and for our little ones, and for all our substance. For I was ashamed to require of the king a band of soldiers and horsemen to help us against the enemy in the way: because we had spoken unto the king, saying, The hand of our God is upon all them for good that seek him; but his power and his wrath is against all them that forsake him. So we fasted and besought our God for this: and he was intreated of us.

schools.summary: Delitzsch reads the straight way as a road cleared of obstructions, takes the little ones as a collective for the whole household, and refuses the rendering powerful wrath, separating the might that conquers enemies from the anger that falls on the wicked; Ellicott names the danger as desert tribes lying in wait for unprotected caravans and hears in the same phrase that whole households went up.
Gill notes that Ezra could have had the escort merely by asking, so great was his standing with the king.

Clarke makes the refusal a matter of consistency, since failure after asking for soldiers would let the heathen call the religion false; Wesley states the rule that public mercies require public prayers and that the fasting was for sin.
Henry grounds the refusal in what Ezra had told the king, guards it against misuse by allowing that proper means may be used, and notes they had no pillar of cloud and fire as their fathers had.

debates.question: What was Ezra seeking when he asked for a right way?

positions.position: A level road, that is a prosperous journey
Commitment of the company to the guidance of providence, in place of the pillar of cloud

debates.question: Was it right to refuse the escort?

positions.position: Yes, since asking would contradict the testimony already given, though proper means may be used where God's honour is not at stake
Yes, because a reverse afterwards would let the heathen conclude the religion was false and vain

outliers.claim: Denies that his power and his wrath is a single phrase meaning powerful wrath; it names the might that conquers enemies and the anger in which it falls on the wicked.

themes: Then I proclaimed a fast there, at the river of Ahava, that we might afflict ourselves before our God, to seek of him a right way for us, and for our little ones, and for all our substance.

For I was ashamed to require of the king a band of soldiers and horsemen to help us against the enemy in the way: because we had spoken unto the king, saying, The hand of our God is upon all them for good that seek him; but his power and his wrath is against all them that forsake him.
So we fasted and besought our God for this: and he was intreated of us.

24.pericope_label: Then I separated twelve of the chief of the priests, Sherebiah, Hashabiah, and ten of their brethren with them, And weighed unto them the silver, and the gold, and the vessels, even the offering of the house of our God, which the king, and his counsellors, and his lords, and all Israel there present, had offered: I even weighed unto their hand six hundred and fifty talents of silver, and silver vessels an hundred talents, and of gold an hundred talents;

schools.summary: Ellicott renders the clause to Sherebiah, making the two Levites partners with an equal number of priests, values the silver and gold at about a million of English money, and says the metals travelled as bars; Delitzsch refuses that rendering on the ground that the two men were Levites of Merari and could not be numbered among chiefs of priests, and explains that all Israel there present means the Israelites found in Babylon who were not going up.
Gill makes the weighing a defence of Ezra's own integrity and of the carriers against any later accusation, and reports from Jarchi and Aben Ezra a hundred silver vessels of a talent apiece.

Clarke reckons the whole consignment at something over a million pounds sterling while conceding that the weights are variously computed, and denies outright that there were a hundred vessels of a talent each.

Henry reads the sequence as prayer seconded by endeavour, notes the change from delivery by number at the first return to delivery by weight here, and records Ezra's own reason for choosing these men, that holy persons are fittest to carry holy things.

debates.question: Were Sherebiah and Hashabiah among the twelve chiefs of the priests?

positions.position: The clause reads to Sherebiah: the two Levites, with ten others, were joined to an equal number of priests
No; they were Levites of the race of Merari, and a dative would put the priests in a servile relation to them

debates.question: What does a hundred talents of silver vessels describe?

positions.position: A hundred vessels, each weighing a talent
The total weight of all the silver vessels together, not a hundred vessels of a talent apiece

outliers.claim: Following Scheuchzer, values the silver alone at over two million two hundred thousand pounds sterling, more than twice the figure Clarke and Ellicott reach for the entire consignment.

themes: Then I separated twelve of the chief of the priests, Sherebiah, Hashabiah, and ten of their brethren with them,

And weighed unto them the silver, and the gold, and the vessels, even the offering of the house of our God, which the king, and his counsellors, and his lords, and all Israel there present, had offered:
I even weighed unto their hand six hundred and fifty talents of silver, and silver vessels an hundred talents, and of gold an hundred talents;

27.pericope_label: Also twenty basons of gold, of a thousand drams; and two vessels of fine copper, precious as gold. And I said unto them, Ye are holy unto the Lord; the vessels are holy also; and the silver and the gold are a freewill offering unto the Lord God of your fathers. Watch ye, and keep them, until ye weigh them before the chief of the priests and the Levites, and chief of the fathers of Israel, at Jerusalem, in the chambers of the house of the Lord. So took the priests and the Levites the weight of the silver, and the gold, and the vessels, to bring them to Jerusalem unto the house of our God.

schools.summary: Ellicott identifies the drams as darics, puts the basons at rather more than a thousand guineas, proposes the Roman orichalcum for the fine copper, and calls the charge to the carriers a unique verse, treasure consecrated and committed to consecrated hands; Delitzsch sets out the terms of the handover and explains that taking the weight means receiving by weight.

Gill values the basons by the weight of the Persian daric on Cumberland's and Bernard's authority, takes the holiness of the vessels to bar any other use, and reads the charge to watch them as a guard against damage and loss.

Clarke admits he cannot tell what the fine copper was, reports the Syriac's Corinthian brass and rejects the legend behind it, and argues from metal he has watched being made that it was a manufactured alloy.

debates.question: What were the two vessels of fine copper, precious as gold?

positions.position: Probably the Roman orichalcum, a metal very highly valued
Unknown; the Syriac calls it the best Corinthian brass, but more likely a manufactured alloy taking the polish of gold

outliers.claim: Reports keeping a specimen of the modern Asiatic alloy exposed to the weather among old iron for twenty years with hardly any tarnish.

themes: Also twenty basons of gold, of a thousand drams; and two vessels of fine copper, precious as gold.
And I said unto them, Ye are holy unto the Lord; the vessels are holy also; and the silver and the gold are a freewill offering unto the Lord God of your fathers.
Watch ye, and keep them, until ye weigh them before the chief of the priests and the Levites, and chief of the fathers of Israel, at Jerusalem, in the chambers of the house of the Lord.
So took the priests and the Levites the weight of the silver, and the gold, and the vessels, to bring them to Jerusalem unto the house of our God.

31.pericope_label: Then we departed from the river of Ahava on the twelfth day of the first month, to go unto Jerusalem: and the hand of our God was upon us, and he delivered us from the hand of the enemy, and of such as lay in wait by the way. And we came to Jerusalem, and abode there three days. Now on the fourth day was the silver and the gold and the vessels weighed in the house of our God by the hand of Meremoth the son of Uriah the priest; and with him was Eleazar the son of Phinehas; and with them was Jozabad the son of Jeshua, and Noadiah the son of Binnui, Levites; By number and by weight of every one: and all the weight was written at that time.

schools.summary: Delitzsch reconciles the twelfth day of departure with the first day appointed for the journey by assigning the interval to the recruiting of Levites, computes the road at three months and a half, admits the distance cannot be determined while Ahava is unlocated, and insists the record made at the handover was an authentic list; Ellicott sums the journey in the phrase the hand of our God was upon us and assigns the three days of rest to private devotion as well.
Gill dates the departure to the twelfth of Nisan, two days before the passover began, and makes the three days at Jerusalem simple recovery from a fatiguing journey.
Henry reckons the journey at about four months, explains the slow marches by the size of the company, and reads the discharge of the trust as both an ease to the mind and an honour to the name.

debates.question: How long did the journey take?

positions.position: Three months and a half, from the twelfth of the first month to the first of the fifth
About four months, the marches slow because the company was large

debates.question: What were the three days at Jerusalem for?

positions.position: Rest and recovery before any business was undertaken
Rest and more private devotion together

outliers.claim: Concedes that the length of road cannot be determined at all, since the particulars of the journey are unrecorded and the site of the river Ahava is unknown.

themes: Then we departed from the river of Ahava on the twelfth day of the first month, to go unto Jerusalem: and the hand of our God was upon us, and he delivered us from the hand of the enemy, and of such as lay in wait by the way.
And we came to Jerusalem, and abode there three days.

Now on the fourth day was the silver and the gold and the vessels weighed in the house of our God by the hand of Meremoth the son of Uriah the priest; and with him was Eleazar the son of Phinehas; and with them was Jozabad the son of Jeshua, and Noadiah the son of Binnui, Levites;
By number and by weight of every one: and all the weight was written at that time.

35.pericope_label: Also the children of those that had been carried away, which were come out of the captivity, offered burnt offerings unto the God of Israel, twelve bullocks for all Israel, ninety and six rams, seventy and seven lambs, twelve he goats for a sin offering: all this was a burnt offering unto the Lord. And they delivered the king’s commissions unto the king’s lieutenants, and to the governors on this side the river: and they furthered the people, and the house of God.

schools.summary: Delitzsch reads the sacrifice numbers as deliberate, twelve for the tribes, ninety-six as eight times twelve and seventy-seven as seven intensified, and sets the sin offering before the burnt offering as its necessary basis; Ellicott finds an order of precedence in the closing verses and separates the satraps in military authority from the governors in civil authority under them.
Gill identifies the offerers as those who came up with Ezra and names the territory of the governors as the provinces beyond the great river.

Clarke observes that only Judah and Benjamin were present as tribes yet a bullock was offered for each of the twelve, and abandons his own Persian etymologies for the word rendered lieutenants; Wesley takes the same numbers as marking the union of the two kingdoms at one altar.

debates.question: What do the twelve bullocks signify when ten tribes were gone?

positions.position: A bullock for every tribe as if present, though only Judah and Benjamin were there in force
The union of the two kingdoms, all twelve meeting by their representatives at one altar
Twelve for all Israel, the twelve tribes, in an offering of gratitude for the restoration

outliers.claim: Withdraws his own proposed Persian derivations for the word rendered lieutenants, saying that where there is so little certainty conjecture is useless.

themes: Also the children of those that had been carried away, which were come out of the captivity, offered burnt offerings unto the God of Israel, twelve bullocks for all Israel, ninety and six rams, seventy and seven lambs, twelve he goats for a sin offering: all this was a burnt offering unto the Lord.
And they delivered the king’s commissions unto the king’s lieutenants, and to the governors on this side the river: and they furthered the people, and the house of God.
